newly_confirmed.position_statement: Evaluating an LLM system is different from evaluating an LLM model — you must evaluate your own system on the task it is meant to solve, not just the base model.

citation.quote: [illustrative] test the system you actually built, not the model in isolation
citation.statement: You have to evaluate the whole system you assembled, not just the raw base model.

net_new.statement: Eval datasets should be version-controlled (kept in git) alongside the application code they test.

citation.quote: [illustrative] keep your evals in git next to the code they test
citation.statement: Your eval datasets should be version-controlled alongside your application code.

newly_contested.position_statement: Manual evaluation is the right place to start; automation scales human judgment but does not replace it.

supporting.quote: The first obvious solution to this complexity is manual evaluations, and honestly that's where you should start.
supporting.statement: Manual evaluation—reading outputs yourself—is the right place to start, since it builds intuition, reveals patterns, and clarifies what 'good' means for your use case.

opposing.quote: [illustrative] don't waste time reading outputs by hand — automate from the start
opposing.statement: Skip manual evaluation entirely and automate grading from day one.

reconciliation.explanation: The two make opposite process recommendations about where evaluation should begin. Position evals-0003 holds that you must start by reading outputs manually to learn what 'good' means before anything can be automated; the new unit holds that manual reading is wasted effort and grading should be automated from the outset. Whether starting manual actually produces better evals than starting automated is a checkable claim about practice, but nothing here resolves it, so it stays contested.
